Comment 2-2: I appreciate the authors for their efforts in testing symmetric cells
using Ce-DTPA and Fe-DTPA electrolytes respectively. However, I am surprised by
the rapid capacity degradation observed in both symmetric cells (Fig. S26), which
contradicts the stable performance reported in Fig. 4e and 4f. This discrepancy
requires explanation to ensure consistency in the reported data.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment.
The observed discrepancy between the symmetric cell results (original Fig. S26) and
the full-cell performance in Fig. 4e and 4f is primarily due to the experimental
limitations during symmetric cell assembly.
To construct the symmetric cells, Fe3+-DTPA and Ce3+-DTPA were first employed as
anolyte and catholyte, respectively, to assemble a Fe3+-Ce3+ DTPA RFB and complete
the initial charging process. Following full charge, Fe3+-DTPA was reduced to Fe2+-
DTPA, which was then used as the catholyte in another symmetrical cell, while fresh
Fe3+-DTPA served as the anolyte. This setup enabled cycling tests for the Fe3+/2+-
DTPA symmetrical RFB. Similarly, after charging, Ce3+-DTPA was oxidized to Ce4+-
DTPA, which was then employed as the anolyte and paired with fresh Ce3+-DTPA
catholyte to form the Ce3+/4+-DTPA symmetrical RFB for subsequent testing.
However, during disassembly and reassembly, it is difficult to completely avoid
exposure to ambient air, especially for Fe2+-DTPA, which is highly sensitive to
oxidation by dissolved oxygen. This unintended exposure leads to partial oxidation of
Fe2+-DTPA prior to test, resulting in artificial capacity fading. Moreover, even trace
amounts of residual air in the symmetric cell chamber can continuously affect redox-
active species during cycling. Similar air-sensitivity issues have also been reported in
other Fe-based aqueous RFB systems, e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 63, e202316593
(2024), https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202316593.
In the initial submission, we used a simplified decoupling strategy with relatively short
cycle numbers (200 cycles) to highlight the distinct CE and VE contributions of Fe-
DTPA and Ce-DTPA, which are more prominent during early cycling—particularly
for Fe-DTPA.
To address the reviewer’s concern and ensure consistency with the full-cell results,
we have re-performed the symmetric cell experiments under improved conditions. All
electrolyte preparation, cell disassembly, and reassembly were carried out strictly
under nitrogen atmosphere using a glovebox setup to minimize oxygen interference.
Furthermore, we extended the cycling duration to 500 cycles to better match the test
conditions in Fig. 4e and 4f. Under these improved conditions, the capacity retention
is significantly enhanced. The updated symmetric cell results are shown in the revised
Fig. S27 as follows.

Comment 2-4: Regarding the extended cycling test, the authors have indicated a
charging limit of up to 70% state of charge (SOC), with a cutoff at 1 V. Is there a
specific rationale for capping the capacity at 70%? From the observed voltage profiles,
it appears that the full cell has been charged to full capacity unless significant voltage
plateaus exist above 1 V, which would justify such limitations. If so, I would encourage
authors to show the testing results by increasing the cut off voltage to a high voltage
value, such as 1.5 V.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important question and suggestion.
Our limiting of charging to 70% SOC (cutoff at 1.0 V) is based on commonly used
operating procedures in iron-based aqueous RFBs since full-depth cycling
(approaching 100% SOC) often leads to excessive overpotential, enhanced side
reactions (e.g., water splitting), and accelerated capacity fade. In practice, the usable
capacity of Fe–Ce DTPA systems is below the theoretical 100% SOC, a 70% SOC
window captures nearly all the reversible capacity while avoiding the high-voltage
regime where polarization and parasitic reactions dominate. As the cell approaches
full charge, the required charging voltage rises sharply due to increased activation and
concentration overpotentials. This high-voltage regime not only accelerates undesired
reactions (notably water splitting) but also impacts the DTPA complex stability.
Limiting SOC to ~70% maintains the cell within a relatively low overpotential
window, minimizing side reactions and extending cycle life—an approach also
adopted in other iron-based flow battery studies (e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 63,
e202316593 (2024), https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202316593; ACS Energy Lett. 9,
3859−3868 (2024), https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.4c01550).
We have added such information on page 11 marked in yellow in the revised
manuscript as follows:
“The longer cycle tests with 15 mL electrolytes were charged at 80 mA·cm−2 to 70%
SOC, or cutoff at 1 V (N211 membrane), avoiding the high-voltage regime where
polarization and parasitic reactions dominate.”
After extended cycling, the polarization increases further, pushing the charge voltage
above the water-splitting threshold. By enforcing a 1.0 V cutoff, we avoid entering the
region where oxygen evolution would occur, thereby protecting both electrode
integrity and electrolyte composition. This behavior is reflected in the gradual capacity
decline observed in Figure S21, where a small drop corresponds to polarization growth
triggering the voltage cutoff.
We adopted the reviewer’s suggestion and performed additional cycling with the
cutoff voltage raised to 1.5 V. The results are shown in the following Figure R1. It can
be observed that although this higher cutoff does allow access to the remaining
capacity, both the CE and EE have decreased, suggesting that high-voltage operation
exacerbates side reactions and will shorten cycle life. Therefore, a 1.0 V cutoff was
used for our study.
